paragraphs: Entry: go long when today's close finishes above the highest daily high of the prior 20 trading days. 03.title: Wait-for-the-Dip — Annual Cash/NIFTY 50 Switch
03.subtitle: Sit in cash from 1 Jan; deploy 100% only if NIFTY 50 closes 10% below its year-start price; withdraw back to cash on 31 Dec. Repeats every year, compounding.
03.source_line: Data: daily OHLC (^NSEI, unadjusted) price data Report generated 2026-08-23 19:30

pills.text: 10% below that reference price
withdrawn at that day's close

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — plain-English recap of the rule being tested.
paragraphs: Every 1 January, the account starts the year entirely in cash (the prior year's ending balance carries forward — returns compound year to year). That year's reference price is NIFTY 50's close on the first trading day of the year. If, on any later day that year, the close falls to "10% below that reference price", 100% of the cash is deployed — filled at the next day's open. The position is then held until the year's last trading day, where it is "withdrawn at that day's close" ("31 Dec"), regardless of price. If the -10% level is never touched that year, the account simply sits in cash all year and earns 0% for it. Only one entry/exit cycle per year — a second dip after a rebound is not re-bought.

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanical reasons behind the headline numbers, stated plainly.
paragraphs: The strategy only deployed cash in 7 of 18 years (39%), and even then only for part of each year — across the whole 2008-01-01–2026-08-21 span it held NIFTY for 29% of the days and sat in cash for the rest. Net return (+105.0% frictionless) is far below buy-and-hold (+294.7%) largely because of that — most of the time, this account earned nothing while the market moved. Its max drawdown is also far shallower (-54.0% vs. -59.9%), but that is mostly a side effect of rarely being invested, not evidence the -10% trigger is a skillful timing signal — a scattering of just 7 events (2 of them losses) is a very small sample to draw a conclusion from either way. Also note the profit is heavily concentrated: the top 5 triggered years account for 162% of total net profit.

04.title: Flight to Midcap — NIFTY 50 / Midcap 150 Rotation
04.subtitle: Hold NIFTY 50 by default. When NIFTY closes 15% below its all-time high, move 100% into midcap for exactly one year, then rotate back to NIFTY. Repeats.

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — plain-English recap of the rule being tested.
paragraphs: The account defaults to 100% NIFTY 50 — unlike the two prior reports, it is never sitting in cash. ATH (all-time high) is NIFTY's own running record closing level, tracked continuously since 2007-09-17 — it only ever rises or holds flat, never resets. Whenever NIFTY's close falls to "15% below that ATH", the account sells all of its NIFTY and buys midcap instead (filled at the next day's open), confirmed in chat as the "NIFTY Midcap 150 tracking ETF, MID150BEES.NS". It then holds midcap for "exactly 365 calendar days", at which point it's a scheduled, known-in-advance event — modelled as switching back to NIFTY at that day's own close, not the next open. Only after that rotation back does the account start watching for the next -15% signal again — starting the following trading day. Because midcap price data only goes back to 2019-02-04, the backtest itself can only run from there, even though the ATH used to judge each dip reflects NIFTY's full history back to 2007-09-17.

panels.heading: Read this before concluding "rotating into midcap works"

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the two most important caveats behind the headline numbers, stated plainly.
paragraphs: Only 3 closed episodes exist in the ~6.5 years this ETF has traded, and all 3 happened to have midcap outperform NIFTY over the year that followed. A 100% win rate on 3 events is an encouraging sign, not evidence of an edge — with a sample this small, a single future counter-example would flip the picture, and there is no statistical basis here to say the -15%/1-year rule is better than chance.

The risk story is not what you might expect. The strategy's worst drawdown (-44.8%) is actually deeper than either static benchmark (-38.4% for NIFTY, -38.4% for midcap) — because the account rotated into the higher-beta midcap segment right as the 2020 COVID crash was still unfolding, and midcap kept falling faster than NIFTY did before the eventual recovery. Buying the dip into a more volatile asset can make the ride down worse before it makes the ride back up better.

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — plain-English recap of the rule, and one judgment call flagged up front.
paragraphs: ₹1,000 is invested every month, on the first trading day, into midcap — filled at that day's own close (a scheduled contribution, not a reactive signal). Separately, midcap's own all-time high (its running record closing level, since 2019-02-04) is tracked continuously. If midcap's close ever falls to "10% below that ATH", an extra ₹5,000 is invested (filled at the next day's open); if it falls to "20% below", a further ₹10,000 is invested on top. Both tiers can fire in the same decline if it's steep enough.

"Judgment call" — the instruction didn't say how often a tier can re-fire. Tested literally (any day the close is ≤10% below ATH), midcap's price wobbled across that exact line 23 separate times in barely two months in mid-2019 alone — each would trigger another ₹5,000. That's almost certainly not the intent, so this report only lets a tier fire again after midcap has set a genuinely new all-time high since it last fired — turning that into a sensible 6 tier-1 and 3 tier-2 events across 2019-02-04–2026-08-21. More sensitivity points (5%, 20%, 25%…) would be needed to say where any real "sweet spot" sits — this report only tested two thresholds.

20.title: Momentum + Gold, With a Drawdown Catch
20.subtitle: 50/50 Midcap150 Momentum-10 + gold — but a 20% drawdown in the momentum leg sells all the gold into momentum, held until a full recovery, then reset back to 50/50.

panels.heading: The rule, and the honest result up front

paragraphs: Start 50% Midcap150 Momentum-10 / 50% gold. The moment the momentum leg falls 20% below its OWN running peak, sell 100% of the gold and put it all into momentum — an all-in lump sum funded by the diversification cushion. Stay 100% momentum until it makes a brand-new all-time high (fully recovers), then reset to exactly 50/50 and repeat. This happened 5 times over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, averaging 237 days to recover each time.

The catch does what it's designed to do on the risk side — shallower drawdown than holding pure momentum alone. But on return, it underperforms simply buying 50/50 once and never touching it again (+31.2% CAGR vs. +35.3%) — and it even underperforms a plain CALENDAR-rebalanced 50/50 blend on drawdown (-29.2% vs. -21.7%). Repeatedly resetting back to 50/50 after each recovery turns out to cap the compounding of the far-faster-growing momentum leg more than the "buy the dip" timing helps — see the honesty note below for the mechanism.

panels.heading: Why "buying the dip" here still lost to doing nothing

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Over 2009-01-02–2026-08-24, momentum alone compounded at +40.5% a year versus gold's +13.9% — momentum grew roughly 403x versus gold's 9x over the full window. A 50/50 split that is NEVER rebalanced naturally drifts to be almost entirely momentum within a few years, simply because the faster-compounding asset dominates the mix — that drift is exactly what "static, never touched" is capturing, and it's a large share of why it wins.

The catch rule does the opposite at every single cycle: the moment momentum recovers from a dip, it forcibly resets the mix back to 50/50 — selling down exactly the asset that was about to keep compounding fastest, and buying back into gold, right as momentum turns UP again. Each of the 5 reset points is a small, repeated tax on the momentum leg's own compounding, paid in exchange for a real but partial reduction in how deep the worst drawdown gets.

That trade-off shows up exactly as expected: the catch's max drawdown (-29.2%) is shallower than pure momentum's (-35.1%) — the rule does work as risk management. It just isn't a free lunch: plain periodic rebalancing, with no drawdown-timing logic at all, achieves an even shallower drawdown (-21.7%) for a similar return give-up, suggesting the discipline of rebalancing itself — not the specific -20%/new-high timing rule — is doing most of the risk reduction here.

22.title: Monthly RSI-70 Crossover Rotation
22.subtitle: Any NSE stock above ₹2,000 Cr market cap — enter the moment its monthly RSI crosses above 70, hold up to 5 positions at once, exit on a 15% stop or month-end, whichever comes first.

paragraphs: Any NSE EQ-series stock with market cap > Rs 2,000 Cr (not restricted to NIFTY 500). "Monthly RSI" is checked EVERY trading day, not just once a month: it's Wilder(14) RSI on monthly closes, re-evaluated daily by treating each day's price as a stand-in for "this month's close so far." A stock enters the moment its RSI crosses above 70 — any day, no minimum pool required to start. Up to 5 positions are held at once; if more stocks cross on one day than there are open slots, the ones that fill the remaining slots are picked at random (not ranked). Each position exits independently on whichever comes first: a 15% drop from ITS OWN entry price, or the last trading day of the month it was entered in.

The stop-loss is checked against each day's LOW (not just the close) and fills at the day's OPEN if price already gapped past -15% overnight — an earlier version of this backtest checked only the close and let losses run to -80/-90% on gap days before the check ever fired. 23.title: Gold/Silver Absolute Momentum Rotation
23.subtitle: Hold gold and/or silver only while each metal's own risk-adjusted 6m/12m momentum is positive; exit that leg to cash the moment it turns negative. Checked and rebalanced monthly.

panels.heading: The rule, and the honest result up front

pills.text: in cash 26% of all months
lags buy-and-hold gold on both return and drawdown

paragraphs: Every month-end, gold (GLD) and silver (SLV) are each scored independently on the exact same risk-adjusted momentum formula used everywhere else in this project — 6-month and 12-month return divided by trailing 1-year volatility, averaged 0.5/0.5 — except here the score is judged against zero, not against a broad universe's cross-sectional average (there are only two assets, too few for a cross-sectional Z-score to mean anything). A metal is held only while its own score is positive; the moment it turns negative, that leg exits fully to cash. Both can be held together (split 50/50 of invested capital), and both can be in cash together.

The honest result: this rule spent 26.3% of all months sitting in some cash, yet still compounded at +7.3% — worse than simply buying and holding gold alone (+10.2%), worse than a static 50/50 gold/silver blend rebalanced monthly (+9.9%), and its max drawdown (-55.3%) is actually deeper than gold's own buy-and-hold drawdown (-45.6%). The exit-to-cash rule did not protect capital here — see the honesty note below for why.

panels.heading: Why exiting to cash didn't protect capital here

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Gold and silver are highly correlated — both are precious metals that mostly rise and fall together on the same macro drivers (real rates, the dollar, safe-haven demand). A momentum rule built for a broad, DIVERSE universe of 30-500+ stocks works because when one stock's trend breaks, dozens of others are usually still working — the portfolio rotates into what's left. With only two, highly correlated assets, there's rarely anywhere for the rule to rotate INTO; when momentum breaks, it mostly means both metals are entering a choppy patch together, and the rule's response is to sit in cash and wait rather than find a new leader.

That shows up directly in the peak-to-trough dates: both the momentum rotation and GLD buy-and-hold peaked on the same day (2011-08-22) — the start of gold's real 2011-2015 bear market. GLD's own drawdown bottomed and began recovering by 2015-12-17. The momentum rule's trough came much later, 2019-05-02 — the monthly re-scoring kept flipping the position in and out of a genuinely choppy, directionless multi-year stretch (2015-2019) that a simple buy-and-hold just rode through without trading at all, each exit/re-entry realizing a small loss it didn't need to take.

The rule spent 26.3% of all months in some amount of cash — capital that earned zero return while it waited, on top of the whipsaw losses from re-entering. For two assets this correlated, being "always in whichever one is stronger" (relative momentum, never cash) or simply buying and holding both would very likely have beaten "get out and wait" — that's an untested alternative for a future report, not a claim proven here.

Yet both thresholds land in almost the same place on drawdown (-32.5% vs. -32.1%) — meaning the EXTRA tail-risk protection the tighter 15% stop is supposedly buying, over and above what 30% already provides, turns out to be worth very little. For this specific strategy, a looser stop (or arguably no stop at all, per the original report 27 finding) is the better risk/reward trade-off than a tight one.

30.title: Midcap Momentum 10 — No Stop-Loss, Just a Breakeven Profit-Lock
30.subtitle: Same exact selection/weighting as reports 11-19, 24, 25, 27 — no downside stop at all. Instead: once a position has run up 30% from entry, arm a protective exit at cost — if it falls all the way back to breakeven before the next rebalance, exit immediately at 0%, rather than riding it down further or waiting.

paragraphs: This rule only ever fires for a position that BOTH ran up 30%+ from entry AND later gave essentially all of that gain back before the next rebalance — a much narrower trigger condition than report 27's fixed-percentage-loss stops. Over 2008-12-31–2026-08-24, that happened to just 19 of 360 positions (5.3%) — versus 15%'s 43.3% and 30%'s 12.5% of positions affected in report 27.

The result is correspondingly small: CAGR barely moves, from +40.6% (original) to +39.6% (with the lock) — a 1.0% point difference, far smaller than either of report 27's stop-loss variants — and max drawdown is essentially unchanged (-35.1% vs. -35.1%). This rule locks in exactly what it's designed to: guaranteeing a big winner can never fully round-trip back to a loss, without materially touching the strategy's overall risk/return profile.

panels.heading: Why this rule barely moves the needle

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Report 27's stop-losses fire on a SINGLE condition (price falls X% from entry) — easy to trigger, which is why 43.3% of positions got caught at a 15% stop. This rule requires TWO conditions in sequence: the position must first prove it can run up 30%, and THEN give essentially all of that entire gain back before the next rebalance. Most positions that reach +30% either keep running (never re-test entry) or pull back only partially — a full round-trip all the way to breakeven is a narrow, specific pattern, which is exactly why it only happened 19 times in 360 positions across 18 years.

What this rule DOES guarantee, on the 19 times it fired, is that a position which was once a big winner can never turn into an outright loss on the way back down — the average locked-out return was -0.3%, almost exactly breakeven by construction. Whether those specific 19 positions would have ended up positive or negative by the ACTUAL next rebalance (had the rule not intervened) isn't shown here — that counterfactual wasn't computed — but given how few positions are affected, either way the portfolio-level impact was always going to be small.

The practical takeaway: this is a genuinely different kind of rule than a stop-loss — it protects a specific outcome (never letting a confirmed winner become a loser) rather than capping downside broadly, and it costs almost nothing to add because it so rarely fires. It is not a substitute for a stop-loss if the goal is limiting how much any single position can lose — for that, report 27's 30% threshold remains the better-tested option.

This report instead tracks each stock's real, uninterrupted tenure in the top 10 as ONE row: it opens the first time the stock is picked (NEW), stays open through every rebalance it's still selected (CARRIED — tagged, not a new row), and closes the moment it's finally dropped (EXITED), with ONE entry price, ONE exit price, and the total gain/loss across the whole run.

Over 2015-01-02–2026-08-24, that's 179 distinct positions instead of the much larger leg-count reports 24/26 would show for the same period — win rate 65.1%, average winner +71.4%, average loser -13.6%. 32.subtitle: Same strategy as reports 11-19/24-27/30-31, no strategy-side stop-loss — but every rebalance now buys 2x the notional per position (50% own capital, 50% borrowed via Kotak Neo's Margin Trading Facility), paying real MTF interest, doubled transaction costs, and modeled margin-call risk.

drawdown roughly doubles too (-59.4% vs -35.1%)

paragraphs: The strategy itself is unchanged — same top-10 selection by 6m/12m risk-adjusted momentum, same equal weighting, same June/December rebalance. What changes: at every rebalance, each position is funded 50% by your own capital and 50% borrowed via Kotak Neo's MTF at +9.7% p.a. — buying 2x the notional exposure per rupee of your own capital. Every real charge Kotak Neo and Indian exchanges actually levy is modeled: brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty, GST, and the MTF interest itself — all sourced and cited below.

The honest result, at the headline 30%-maintenance-margin assumption: CAGR rises from the frictionless +40.6% to +51.9% — well short of a clean 2x — while max drawdown deepens from -35.1% to -59.4%. 52 of 360 positions (14.4%) got forcibly liquidated by a margin call before ever reaching their scheduled rebalance, averaging a -59.9% loss on capital each time. See the honesty note below for why the maintenance-margin assumption itself changes this picture substantially — and why a LOOSER threshold isn't automatically safer.

panels.heading: Why 2x leverage doesn't give you 2x the return — and why looser margin isn't automatically safer

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Ignoring costs and margin calls entirely, doubling each position's exposure would compound to roughly double the frictionless strategy's already-large multiple — arithmetically much more than "2x the CAGR" once compounded over 36 rebalances, since leverage amplifies BOTH the size of each period's gain and the base it compounds from. Real MTF eats into that in three separate ways: +0.24% + +0.22% of round-trip transaction costs on DOUBLE the notional (vs. cash), +9.69% p.a. interest on the borrowed half (averaging 4.37% of a position's own capital per ~6-month hold), and — the big one — margin calls that force-crystallize a loss at the worst possible moment instead of letting a position ride out a temporary dip.

That third effect is why the maintenance-margin ASSUMPTION matters so much, and why the relationship isn't what you'd first guess. At a 40% maintenance threshold (margin calls fire on roughly a 23.1%-37.5% range of price drops depending on the exact threshold — see the table above), 133 of 360 positions (36.9%) got force-sold — MORE than three times as often as at 20% maintenance (21 calls, 5.8%). A tighter (lower) maintenance requirement gives a volatile momentum stock more room to have an ordinary bad month WITHOUT being forced out — which is exactly why the 20% scenario ends up with the HIGHEST CAGR of the three (+59.5%) despite being the "loosest" margin rule, and the 40% scenario the lowest (+37.5%) despite being the "safest"-sounding one.

None of the three scenarios avoid a deep drawdown, though — all three land between -62.3% and -59.4%, meaningfully worse than the frictionless strategy's own -35.1%. The margin-call mechanism changes WHEN and HOW OFTEN losses get crystallized, but 2x leverage on an already-volatile momentum strategy is a deeper hole to climb out of under every assumption tested here.

paragraphs: Subtracting NIFTY 50's own return from every stock's return before ranking shifts every stock's number by the SAME amount that day — which, on its own, wouldn't change the ranking at all (subtracting a constant preserves rank order). What actually changes the outcome is that this shift happens BEFORE dividing by each stock's own (different) volatility — so the same constant shift affects a low-volatility stock's ratio more than a high-volatility stock's. The only reason relative momentum picks a DIFFERENT top 10 at all is that this shift happens before dividing by each stock's OWN volatility, which differs stock to stock: a low-volatility stock's score moves more (in ratio terms) from the same absolute shift than a high-volatility stock's does. That's a real effect, but a second-order one — which is exactly why 92.2% of picks stay the same, versus only 59.3% for report 33's skip-month variant, which changes the entire reference date every calculation is anchored to (a first-order effect, not a second-order one).

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.

57.subtitle: Reports 42-56 triggered the cash/invested switch purely from NIFTY 50's own 200-day EMA. This report adds a second condition: NIFTY 50 must be above its own 200-EMA AND at least a minimum share of the relevant top-10 candidates must ALSO be above their own 200-day EMA — so one index's price alone isn't the sole trigger. Four thresholds tested (30%/50%/70%/90%), same Midcap150 Momentum 10 formula throughout.

pills.text: barely moves the needle at any reasonable threshold

paragraphs: At 30%, 50%, and 70% breadth thresholds, CAGR and max drawdown are essentially IDENTICAL to the NIFTY-50-only filter (+38.3% / -23.5%) — the breadth condition is almost always already satisfied whenever NIFTY 50 itself is above its 200-EMA. Only at a strict 90% threshold does the filter start behaving noticeably differently, and even then it's WORSE, not better: re-entries climb to 82 (vs. 69 for NIFTY-only) for essentially the same CAGR and drawdown.

The honest reading: in this Midcap150 universe, breadth and NIFTY 50's own trend are highly correlated — when the broad market is above its 200-day average, more than half (often more than 70%) of midcap stocks tend to be too, simply because they're all reacting to the same broad economic and market conditions. Requiring extra breadth confirmation adds complexity without adding much genuinely NEW information, at least at the thresholds tested here.

panels.heading: Why breadth confirmation didn't add much here

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Breadth confirmation is a real, commonly-used idea in technical analysis — the logic is that a "healthy" market advance should be broad, not just a few large names pulling the index up while everything else lags, and a market where the index looks fine but breadth is deteriorating underneath is sometimes flagged as an early warning sign. That logic didn't pay off here because Midcap150 and NIFTY 50, despite trading different stocks, are both driven by the SAME broad economic and liquidity conditions — interest rates, FII flows, macro sentiment — so their trend signals move together far more often than they diverge. A confirmation rule only helps when the two signals genuinely disagree often enough to matter, and in this dataset, they mostly don't.

The 90% threshold's slightly WORSE result (more re-entries for no better CAGR or drawdown) is itself instructive: a very strict breadth requirement doesn't wait for a genuinely different signal, it just makes the SAME underlying NIFTY-50 signal jumpier, since requiring near-unanimous participation is itself sensitive to whichever single stock happens to be right at its own 200-EMA on a given day. This is a cautionary example against reflexively adding "confirmation" conditions without checking whether they're independent enough of the base signal to actually change anything.

58.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Per-Stock Trailing Stop vs. Report 27's Fixed Stop
58.subtitle: Report 27 tested a FIXED stop-loss (15% and 30% below each position's own ENTRY price, never moving). This report tests the same two thresholds measured off each position's own PEAK price since entry instead — a trailing stop that ratchets UP as a winning position's peak rises, cutting individual losers without needing report 42-57's portfolio-wide regime switch at all. Same realistic Low/Open fill methodology as report 27, cash until the next rebalance.

pills.text: a tight trailing stop is far more destructive than a tight fixed one
15% trailing stopped out 90.0% of ALL positions

paragraphs: At 15%, trailing is dramatically WORSE than fixed: CAGR collapses from +23.6% (fixed) to +8.8% (trailing) — because a stop that RATCHETS UP with every new high triggers on completely normal volatility, not just genuine reversals. It stopped out 90.0% of every position ever held, at an AVERAGE return of +2.4% — often a small gain, not a loss, because the stop was simply too tight to survive ordinary price noise.

At 30%, the picture flips: trailing BEATS fixed on drawdown — -32.1% (fixed) improves to -29.4% (trailing) — for a modest CAGR cost, +35.0% to +31.3%. A WIDE trailing stop genuinely locks in gains on winners without over-triggering; a TIGHT one just adds noise-driven churn.

panels.heading: Why "trailing" isn't automatically "better"

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A fixed stop is anchored to the ENTRY price for the whole holding period — a stock that rallies 40% then pulls back 15% from its peak is nowhere near a 15%-off-entry fixed stop (it's still up ~19% from entry), so it survives. A TRAILING stop has no such cushion: the moment that same stock's peak rises, the stop level rises right along with it, so a routine 15% pullback from ANY new high — completely normal for a volatile midcap stock, several times a year even during a genuine uptrend — triggers an exit. That's exactly why 90.0% of every position held was stopped out at 15% trailing, at a barely-positive average return: the stop was firing on ordinary noise, not on actual reversals.

A wide trailing stop (30%) avoids that failure mode — normal volatility rarely swings 30% from a recent peak within a 6-month window, so it mostly triggers on genuine, sustained reversals, which is exactly the scenario where locking in a rising floor pays off. The lesson generalizes beyond stop-losses: any rule that reacts to a MOVING reference point (a trailing peak, a moving average, a recent high) needs to be set wide enough to filter out routine noise, or it ends up reacting to volatility itself rather than to the trend it was meant to protect against — the same lesson report 46 found for EMA span and report 47 found for confirmation delay.

59.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Asymmetric EMA Regime Filter
59.subtitle: Reports 42-58 used the SAME 200-day EMA for both exiting and re-entering. This report tests exiting on the slow 200-day EMA (unchanged, avoids whipsaw on the way out) but re-entering on a FASTER 50-day EMA — the idea being to catch a market recovery sooner instead of waiting for the slow average to catch up, directly targeting the "always re-enters late" pattern flagged in reports 42, 55, and 56.

panels.heading: Why "catch the recovery sooner" backfires

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: A 50-day EMA is much choppier than a 200-day one — it crosses back and forth across the price far more often, which is exactly why it's faster to react in the first place. The problem is that "faster to react" cuts both ways: it re-enters at the first sign of strength, but a first sign of strength during a bear market is very often a temporary bounce, not a genuine turn. The exit condition is STILL the slow 200-day EMA, so once that false start reverses, the position has to fall a meaningful amount further before the slow exit signal triggers again — the asymmetry doesn't add a fast exit to match the fast entry, it just adds MORE round trips into declines that haven't finished yet.

This is a useful lesson about combining signals of different speeds: pairing a fast trigger with a slow one doesn't automatically get "the best of both" — it can just import the fast signal's false-positive rate into a strategy that was otherwise built around the slow signal's reliability.

62.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Absolute Momentum Gate
62.subtitle: Classic dual-momentum idea: only hold a stock if ITS OWN 12-month return is positive, even if it ranks in the top 10 by RELATIVE momentum against its peers. A slot with no qualifying candidate sits in cash (0% return) rather than being filled by the next-best relatively-ranked stock regardless of its own direction. Same selection formula and ranking otherwise, same top 10, same June/December schedule.

pills.text: the gate almost never fires, so almost nothing changes
only 1 of 36 rebalances ever had an unfilled slot

paragraphs: Drawdown is IDENTICAL to the original (-35.1% either way), and CAGR is slightly WORSE: +40.6% to +40.3%. Across 36 rebalances, the gate excluded a candidate in only 1 of them, averaging 9.86 of 10 slots filled.

The reason: a stock that ranks in the top 10 by RELATIVE momentum out of 150 midcap names is, in a normal market, very likely already up over the past year — the relative ranking and the absolute-return gate are checking almost the same thing most of the time. The gate only bites in the rare, extreme scenario where very few stocks in the whole universe are up at all (right after a severe crash) — and even then, it costs a little return without changing the drawdown outcome at all.

panels.heading: Why relative and absolute momentum mostly agree

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Dual momentum (relative ranking PLUS an absolute-return gate) is a well-known idea specifically because in some asset classes and time periods, the two disagree often enough to matter — e.g. picking the "least bad" of a set of assets that are ALL falling, which an absolute gate would correctly veto. Report 35's bottom-10 reversal sanity check already showed something related: even this project's WORST-ranked picks still beat NIFTY 50 on this dataset, suggesting a general midcap risk premium runs through nearly the whole universe most of the time, not just the top of it. That same effect is likely why the absolute gate barely fires here — when the broad universe is up, the RELATIVE top 10 is almost always ALSO absolute-positive, so the gate has almost nothing to veto.

The one rebalance where it did bite (5 of 10 slots filled) was very likely the December 2008 or June 2009 window, in the immediate aftermath of the global financial crisis — exactly the kind of moment dual momentum is designed to protect against. That it only fires there, and still doesn't move the drawdown number, suggests the strategy's EXISTING risk-adjustment (dividing by trailing volatility) is already doing most of the work an absolute gate would otherwise add.

65.title: Midcap150 Momentum 10 — Volatility-Scaled (Smooth) Exposure
65.subtitle: Reports 42-64's regime filter flips 100%/0% the instant NIFTY 50 crosses its 200-day EMA. This report replaces the hard switch with a CONTINUOUS ramp: exposure scales linearly from 100% (at or above the EMA) down to 0% (a band_pct below it), removing the whipsaw problem at its root rather than tuning around it — there is no discrete state here at all, so there is nothing to "re-enter" or "confirm." Three band widths tested (10%/15%/20%) against the original and report 42's binary filter, all on the identical window.

pills.text: beats the binary filter on CAGR at every band width

paragraphs: Every band tested gives a HIGHER CAGR than the binary filter — +38.5% (binary) vs. +39.5% (10% band), +39.8% (15%), and +40.0% (20%) — while still cutting drawdown meaningfully versus no filter at all (-35.1%): -26.1%, -27.5%, and -28.3% respectively.

The trade-off: none of these bands protect drawdown as deeply as the binary filter's -23.5%. This forms a clean, non-dominated frontier — no filter (best CAGR, worst drawdown) → wider band → narrower band → binary filter (worst CAGR, best drawdown) — with every point on it a genuinely different, reasonable choice depending on how much an investor weights return versus downside protection, not a single "best" answer.

panels.heading: Why removing the whipsaw at its root pays off

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: The binary filter's own honesty notes (reports 42, 46, 47) repeatedly found that its biggest hidden cost is 69 whipsaw round-trips — full sells and full buys triggered by ordinary volatility near the 200-EMA, all charged nothing in this frictionless model but expensive in reality. A smooth ramp has NO discrete flip to whipsaw on: a day where price wobbles slightly above and below the EMA just nudges exposure a few percentage points, rather than triggering a full round-trip. Removing that specific cost is exactly why the smooth version's CAGR comes out ahead of the binary filter's at every band width tested, even though the binary filter still protects drawdown more deeply (it goes all the way to 0% exposure at the depth of a real crash, which the smooth version with a narrow band width only approaches asymptotically).

This IS still a genuinely different mechanism worth weighing, not a strict improvement: the 3.3% of days at fully zero exposure under the tightest (10%) band shows it still fully de-risks during the depths of a real crash, just via a smoother path in and out rather than a single hard switch.

73.title: Midcap150 Momentum 50 — A Much Wider Basket, Same Formula
73.subtitle: Every other report in this project's flagship line picks the top 10 out of Midcap150 by momentum score. This report changes exactly one thing — top_n from 10 to 50, roughly a third of the entire 150-stock universe — using the identical formula, price history, and June/December rebalance schedule, to see what a much broader basket does to CAGR and drawdown.

paragraphs: Widening the basket from top-10 to top-50 cuts CAGR from +40.6% to +30.6% — and drawdown gets slightly WORSE too, not better: -35.1% (top-10) vs. -36.8% (top-50). There's no diversification trade-off to point to here — this isn't "lower return, lower risk," it's lower return with no risk benefit at all.

The likely reason: momentum's edge comes specifically from the STRONGEST-ranked names — diluting the portfolio with names ranked 11th to 50th (weaker momentum scores, by definition) pulls in stocks the formula itself considers less attractive, without actually smoothing out the concentrated portfolio's stock-specific risk enough to show up in max drawdown.

panels.heading: Why concentration wins here

pills.text: framing

panels.what_this_shows: WHAT THIS SHOWS — the mechanism, not just the scoreboard.
paragraphs: Momentum investing's entire premise is that recent relative strength predicts near-term future strength — which means the formula's OWN ranking is claiming stock #1 is a better bet than stock #50. Concentrating in the top-10 takes that claim at face value; diversifying out to top-50 means holding 40 more names the formula itself ranks weaker, which should mechanically drag CAGR toward the broader index's own return — consistent with what happened here (+30.6%, well below top-10's +40.6% but still well above NIFTY 50's +12.7%).

The surprising part is that drawdown didn't improve at all despite the extra breadth — a broader basket is usually expected to smooth out single-stock blowups. That it didn't here suggests Midcap150's worst drawdowns in this window were broad, market-wide moves (most stocks falling together) rather than a few concentrated single-name disasters that diversification would have diluted.

        the full CAGR/drawdown curve between them (e.g. top-7, top-12 weren't tested), and report 73 already covers the
        much-wider top-50 case separately.

Equal weighting within each basket (each of the 5, 10, or 15 names gets an equal share at every
        rebalance) — a 5-stock basket is meaningfully more concentrated per-name (20% each) than a 15-stock one (~6.7% each),
        which is itself part of why their risk profiles differ, separate from the momentum-ranking effect discussed above.

Zero transaction costs on any regime switch or scheduled rebalance — same disclosed omission as
        every other reconstruction here.

Today's fixed Midcap150 constituent list is applied retroactively across the whole window
        (survivorship bias). No F&O-eligibility screen, unadjusted prices, no dividends modeled — same as every other
        reconstruction here.
